flawed_step: The claim assumes triangle-freeness keeps the chromatic number at most 4. It does not: the Mycielski construction gives triangle-free graphs with any chromatic number you want.
counterexample:
Mycielskian: for a graph G on v1..vn, M(G) keeps G, adds new vertices u1..un and one vertex w. Each ui is joined to every neighbour vj of vi, and w is joined to every ui.
(1) M(G) is triangle-free when G is. The ui form an independent set, so a triangle contains at most one ui. If a triangle contains w, it needs two adjacent u's, which is impossible. If a triangle is ui,vj,vk, then vj and vk are adjacent neighbours of vi, so vi,vj,vk is a triangle in G.
(2) If chi(G)=k then chi(M(G)) is at least k+1. Suppose M(G) has a proper k-colouring, and let w have colour k. No ui has colour k. Recolour every vi that has colour k with the colour of ui. The result is proper on G: two recoloured vertices vi,vj cannot be adjacent, since both had colour k. If vi is recoloured and vj is an unrecoloured neighbour, then vj is adjacent to ui, so their colours differ. That gives a (k-1)-colouring of G, a contradiction.
Explicit graph: C5 (triangle-free, chi=3), then M(C5), the 11-vertex Grötzsch graph (triangle-free, chi at least 4), then H=M(M(C5)) on 23 vertices. H is triangle-free with chi(H) at least 5, so H is not 4-colourable.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Apply the Mycielski construction twice to C5 to get a 23-vertex graph. It is triangle-free and has chromatic number 5, because each step keeps the graph triangle-free and raises the chromatic number by at least one; both facts are checked above. So this graph is not 4-colourable.
